title: Test: Workload Placement
summary: Check what you learned across the whole chapter.

questions.q: The section **The Boundary Contract** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: WCET comes from static analysis, measurement plus margin, hybrid methods, or probabilistic tail models, and local worst cases do not compose to a global one on modern microarchitectures.

On a shared die sustained inference drives the junction past the trip point, the governor cuts the clock so every tick overruns its bound, and hysteresis holds the clock down for seconds after the burst ends.
Execution budgets depend on the assurance level, so when a high-criticality task exhausts its lower budget the scheduler withdraws service from low-criticality work to keep the enforcer's tick.

The exchange has two separately timed obligations (board-link transport, then one bounded local publication read inside the WCET), and liveness needs a windowed watchdog that catches early feeds as well as late ones.

questions.q: The section **The Silicon Substrate** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Memory arbiters schedule bursts, not averages, so a safety read waits on the backlog ahead of it and the controller's policy, and shared-cache miss handling, not bandwidth, threatens the declared bound.
Privilege checks govern digital access while the shared rail powers the gates that perform them, so droop, clock faults, and shared resets are failure domains beneath privilege.
A static-partitioning hypervisor binds cores, memory, and peripherals to isolated partitions at boot and colors caches, the standard pattern for a real-time enclave on a shared die.

Couplings act on different timescales (nanosecond droop, microsecond queueing, millisecond ticks, second-scale throttling, hour-scale chassis heat), which tells a rail-correlated fault from a temperature-correlated one.
